To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the model is able to reproduce experimental data, the most important factor determining the spatial extent of outcrossing is source–crop size, and the most effective method of regulation is isolation distance for self–fertility crops.
the isolation distance for oilseed rape is dependent on the fertility of the target crop and the size of the source crop, and is most effective for a self–fertiles crop.

the spatial distribution of gene flow from a genetically modified oilseed rape source crop to a non–modified target crop can be predicted by a mathematical model that combines pollen dispersal, pollination and reproductive processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model that predicts pollen dispersal and the resulting outcrossing between GM and non–GM populations of oilseed–rape.
the development and application of a mathematical model of pollen–driven gene flow in oilseed rape.
the development of a model for predicting the spatial pattern of pollen–mediation gene flow in the environment and the application of the model for the risk assessment of oilseed rape.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the model is useful for predicting the spatial distribution of GM pollen in a range of scenarios and that the model is robust to changes in the parameters used to represent the processes of pollen production, dispersal, deposition and pollination.
gene flow between oilseed rape crops is a complex and variable process.
gene flow from a small source crop is likely to be restricted, and that the risk of gene flow to a target crop can be reduced to an acceptable level by appropriate isolation distances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial distribution of gene flow from a GM crop is dependent on both the source and target crop.
the model is a robust and useful tool to predict the spatial pattern of gene flow from GM crops.
the model provides a reliable and flexible tool to predict pollen–mediated outcrossing between oilseed rape populations and to assess the effects of regulatory measures to reduce this gene flow.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of wind and insect activity is sufficient to explain the observed spatial distribution of out-crossing.
the model is a useful tool for risk assessment and that the results of this work will be used as the basis of a computer program to be used by regulatory agencies.
the risk assessment and regulation for pollen–mediated GM gene flow should be based on a quantitative understanding of the processes that determine the extent of outcrossing.
